Homarus gammarus , known as the European lobster or common lobster , is a species of clawed lobster from the eastern Atlantic Ocean , Mediterranean Sea and parts of the Black Sea . It is closely related to the American lobster , H. americanus . It may grow to a length of 60 cm ( 24 in ) and a mass of 6 kilograms ( 13 lb ) , and bears a conspicuous pair of claws . In life , the lobsters are blue , only becoming " lobster red " on cooking . Mating occurs in the summer , producing eggs which are carried by the females for up to a year before hatching into planktonic larvae . Homarus gammarus is a highly esteemed food , and is widely caught using lobster pots , mostly around the British Isles . 
 Homarus gammarus is a large crustacean , with a body length up to 60 centimetres ( 24 in ) and weighing up to 5 – 6 kilograms ( 11 – 13 lb ) , although the lobsters caught in lobster pots are usually 23 – 38 cm ( 9 – 15 in ) long and weigh 0 @.@ 7 – 2 @.@ 2 kg ( 1 @.@ 5 – 4 @.@ 9 lb ) . Like other crustaceans , lobsters have a hard exoskeleton which they must shed in order to grow , in a process called ecdysis ( moulting ) . This may occur several times a year for young lobsters , but decreases to once every 1 – 2 years for larger animals . 
 The first pair of pereiopods is armed with a large , asymmetrical pair of claws . The larger one is the " crusher " , and has rounded nodules used for crushing prey ; the other is the " cutter " , which has sharp inner edges , and is used for holding or tearing the prey . Usually , the left claw is the crusher , and the right is the cutter . 
 The exoskeleton is generally blue above , with spots that coalesce , and yellow below . The red colour associated with lobsters only appears after cooking . This occurs because , in life , the red pigment astaxanthin is bound to a protein complex , but the complex is broken up by the heat of cooking , releasing the red pigment . 
 The closest relative of H. gammarus is the American lobster , Homarus americanus . The two species are very similar , and can be crossed artificially , although hybrids are unlikely to occur in the wild since their ranges do not overlap .  Female H. gammarus reach sexual maturity when they have grown to a carapace length of 80 – 85 millimetres ( 3 @.@ 1 – 3 @.@ 3 in ) , whereas males mature at a slightly smaller size . Mating typically occurs in summer between a recently moulted female , whose shell is therefore soft , and a hard @-@ shelled male . The female carries the eggs for up to 12 months , depending on the temperature , attached to her pleopods . Females carrying eggs are said to be " berried " and can be found throughout the year . 
 The eggs hatch at night , and the larvae swim to the water surface where they drift with the ocean currents , preying on zooplankton . This stage involves three moults and lasts for 15 – 35 days . After the third moult , the juvenile takes on a form closer to the adult , and adopts a benthic lifestyle . The juveniles are rarely seen in the wild , and are poorly known , although they are known to be capable of digging extensive burrows . It is estimated that only 1 larva in every 20 @,@ 000 survives to the benthic phase . When they reach a carapace length of 15 mm ( 0 @.@ 59 in ) , the juveniles leave their burrows and start their adult lives .

It is also present in most of the Mediterranean Sea , only missing from the section east of Crete , and along only the north @-@ west coast of the Black Sea .  The species can be divided into four genetically distinct populations , one widespread population , and three which have diverged due to small effective population sizes , possibly due to adaptation to the local environment . The first of these is the population of lobsters from northern Norway , which have been referred to as the " midnight @-@ sun lobster " . The populations in the Mediterranean Sea are distinct from those in the Atlantic Ocean . The last distinct population is found in the Netherlands : samples from the <unk> were distinct from those collected in the North Sea or English Channel . 
 Attempts have been made to introduce H. gammarus to New Zealand , alongside other European species such as the edible crab , Cancer pagurus . Between 1904 and 1914 , one million lobster larvae were released from hatcheries in Dunedin , but the species did not become established there . 
 Adult H. gammarus live on the continental shelf at depths of 0 – 150 metres ( 0 – 492 ft ) , although not normally deeper than 50 m ( 160 ft ) . They prefer hard substrates , such as rocks or hard mud , and live in holes or crevices , emerging at night to feed .

 Air Vice Marshal Frank Headlam , CB , CBE ( 15 July 1914 – 23 December 1976 ) was a senior commander in the Royal Australian Air Force ( RAAF ) . Born and educated in Tasmania , he joined the RAAF as an air cadet in January 1934 . He specialised in flying instruction and navigation before the outbreak of World War II . In April 1941 , he became commanding officer of No. 2 Squadron , which operated Lockheed Hudsons . The squadron was deployed to Dutch Timor in December , and saw action against Japanese forces in the South West Pacific . After returning to Australia in February 1942 , Headlam held staff appointments and training commands , finishing the war a group captain . 
 Headlam served as Officer Commanding North @-@ Western Area in 1946 , and as Director of Training from 1947 to 1950 . In 1950 – 51 , during the Malayan Emergency , he was stationed at Singapore as commander of No. 90 ( Composite ) Wing and , later , RAF Tengah . He twice served as acting Air Member for Personnel , in 1957 and 1959 – 60 , receiving appointment as a Commander of the Order of the British Empire in 1958 . Promoted air vice marshal , he successively held the positions of Air Officer Commanding ( AOC ) Operational Command in 1961 – 62 , AOC No. 224 Group RAF from 1962 to 1965 during the Indonesia – Malaysia Konfrontasi , Deputy Chief of the Air Staff in 1965 – 66 , and AOC Support Command in 1966 – 67 . He was appointed a Companion of the Order of the Bath in 1965 . Following a posting to London as Head of the Australian Joint Services Staff from 1968 to 1971 , he retired from the Air Force and died in Melbourne five years later . 
 The son of farmers Malcolm and Hilda Headlam , Frank Headlam was born on 15 July 1914 in Launceston , Tasmania . He was schooled at <unk> College , Hobart , and matriculated in 1932 . He underwent flying instruction with No. 1 Flying Training School ( FTS ) at RAAF Point Cook , Victoria , and was commissioned as a pilot officer on 1 January 1935 .

No larger than a flight according to the official history of the pre @-@ war RAAF , Seaplane Squadron was part of No. 1 FTS and operated Supermarine Southampton flying boats and de Havilland Gipsy Moth floatplanes , among other types . During this posting Headlam was promoted to flying officer , on 1 July 1935 , and wrote a paper on national defence in which he suggested that with " strong air forces , naval forces ( including submarines ) , and fixed defences , Australia may be made practically invulnerable " . According to Air Force historian Alan Stephens , this paper " in effect , defined the ' anti @-@ lodgment ' concept which has been a persistent feature of RAAF strategic thinking " . 
 Headlam completed a flying instructors course in July 1936 and joined the staff of No. 1 FTS . He was promoted to flight lieutenant on 1 March 1937 . Commencing in July 1938 , he was one of six students to take part in the RAAF 's first Long Specialist Navigation Course , run by Flight Lieutenants Bill Garing and Alister Murdoch at Point Cook . The course involved several epic training flights that attracted considerable media attention , including a twelve @-@ day , 10 @,@ 800 @-@ kilometre ( 6 @,@ 700 mi ) round @-@ Australia trip by three Avro Ansons , one of which was piloted by Headlam , in November . The following month , Headlam led the three Ansons on a six @-@ day journey back and forth over Central Australia . He subsequently passed the navigation course with a special distinction . On 27 January 1939 he was posted to RAAF Station Laverton , Victoria , as a flight commander . He served initially with No. 2 Squadron , before transferring to No. 1 Squadron on 29 August . Both units operated Ansons . 
 Following the outbreak of World War II , No. 1 Squadron was engaged in convoy escort and maritime reconnaissance duties off south @-@ eastern Australia . Headlam continued to serve with the squadron as a flight commander until 15 January 1940 , when he was assigned to Headquarters Laverton as the station navigation officer . On 27 March he was posted to the staff of RAAF Headquarters , Melbourne . He was promoted to squadron leader on 1 June 1940 . Two weeks later he married Katherine Bridge at St Paul 's Anglican Church in Frankston ; the couple would have a son and a daughter . 
 Headlam was given command of No. 2 Squadron at Laverton on 15 April 1941 , and raised to wing commander on 1 July . Equipped with Lockheed Hudsons , the squadron mainly conducted maritime patrols in southern waters until 5 December , when four of its aircraft were ordered to Darwin , Northern Territory , in response to fears of Japanese aggression in the Pacific . On 7 December , this detachment established itself at Penfui , near Koepang in Dutch Timor , while No. 2 Squadron 's eight remaining Hudsons were stationed at Darwin on standby . The following day , aware that Australia was now at war in the Pacific , one of the Penfui @-@ based Hudsons attacked the Japanese <unk> Nanyo Maru , which was suspected of being a radio ship , and forced it aground . By 12 December , Headlam had transferred to Penfui as commanding officer of the base , as well as No. 2 Squadron .

Eastern Area Command , considered a de facto operational headquarters owing to the preponderance of combat units under its control , was reorganised as Home Command in October 1953 . He was promoted to acting air commodore in May . His appointment as aide @-@ de @-@ camp to Queen Elizabeth II was announced on 7 October 1954 . 
 Headlam was promoted to substantive air commodore on 1 January 1955 . In November he was posted to RAAF Overseas Headquarters , London , and the following year undertook studies at the Imperial Defence College . Returning to Australia , he served as acting Air Member for Personnel at the Department of Air , Canberra , from 19 March to 21 October 1957 , between the terms of Air Vice Marshals Fred Scherger and Allan Walters , and again from 24 August 1959 to 28 March 1960 , between the terms of Walters and Air Vice Marshal Bill Hely . In this role Headlam occupied a seat on the Air Board , the service 's controlling body that comprised its senior officers and was chaired by the Chief of the Air Staff . He was also one of two RAAF representatives to serve on a committee , chaired by businessman William John Allison , examining conditions of defence service ; the committee 's recommendations led to a doubling of flight pay , among other improvements . Headlam 's other positions at the Department of Air included Air Commodore Plans from October 1957 to January 1959 , and Director General Plans and Policy from January to August 1959 . The latter assignment put him in charge of the RAAF 's Directorate of Intelligence . Headlam was appointed a Commander of the Order of the British Empire ( CBE ) in the 1958 Queen 's Birthday Honours , gazetted on 3 June . In May 1960 he became acting Deputy Chief of the Air Staff . 
 On 30 January 1961 , Headlam joined the staff of Operational Command ( OPCOM ) , the successor organisation to Home Command , responsible for the direction of RAAF operational units . He took over as Air Officer Commanding ( AOC ) OPCOM from Air Vice Marshal Val Hancock in April . Headlam was promoted to air vice marshal on 29 May . On 17 July 1962 , he was posted to RAAF Base Butterworth , Malaya , and took up the appointment of AOC No. 224 Group RAF in Singapore one week later . He was succeeded as AOC OPCOM by Air Vice Marshal Alister Murdoch . As AOC No. 224 Group , Headlam had overall responsibility for regional air defence and offensive air operations during the Brunei Rebellion in December 1962 , and the subsequent Konfrontasi between Indonesia and Malaysia that officially began the following month . Divorced from his first wife in 1956 , he married widowed social worker Vernon Spence at the Sydney registry office on 20 January 1964 . He handed over No. 224 Group to Air Vice Marshal Christopher Foxley @-@ Norris on 30 November . 
 Returning to Australia , Headlam became Deputy Chief of the Air Staff ( DCAS ) on 26 January 1965 . He was appointed a Companion of the Order of the Bath ( CB ) " in recognition of distinguished service in the Borneo Territories " on 22 June . His tenure as DCAS coincided with the most significant rearmament program the Air Force had undertaken since World War II , and with manpower shortages stemming from this expansion and from Australia 's increasing involvement in the security of South East Asia . The first RAAF helicopters were committed to the Vietnam War towards the end of his term , and he travelled to Saigon with the Chief of the General Staff , Lieutenant General Sir John Wilton , in March 1966 to plan the deployment . The year before , Wilton had recommended to Air Marshal Murdoch , the Chief of the Air Staff , that two Iroquois be sent to Vietnam for familiarisation purposes ; Murdoch had rebuffed Wilton , and the RAAF helicopter squadron was considered underprepared for its army co @-@ operation role when it finally did deploy . On 1 January 1968 , Headlam was posted to London as Head of the Australian Joint Services Staff . He served as an Extra Gentleman Usher to the Queen from 17 November 1970 to 5 June 1971 . 
 Returning to Australia in June 1971 , Headlam took resettlement leave before retiring from the Air Force on 3 August . He made his home in Melbourne , where he died aged 62 on 23 December 1976 , after a lengthy battle with cancer . Survived by his children and his second wife , he was given a private funeral and cremated at Springvale Crematorium .

 The current M @-@ 82 dates back to 1926 . It ran from US 31 in Hart to the northern junction of US 131 and M @-@ 46 in Howard City . rewritten: Homarus gammarus, commonly referred to as the European or common lobster, is a species of clawed lobster found in the eastern Atlantic Ocean, the Mediterranean Sea, and parts of the Black Sea. It is closely related to the American lobster, H. americanus. This species can grow up to 60 cm (24 in) in length and weigh up to 6 kilograms (13 lb), characterized by its prominent claws. While alive, these lobsters are blue, turning "lobster red" only after being cooked. Mating takes place in the summer, resulting in eggs that females carry for up to a year before they hatch into planktonic larvae. Homarus gammarus is highly prized as a delicacy and is predominantly caught using lobster pots, especially around the British Isles.

Homarus gammarus is a sizable crustacean, reaching body lengths of up to 60 centimeters (24 inches) and weighing between 5 and 6 kilograms (11 to 13 pounds). However, lobsters typically caught in traps are usually 23 to 38 cm (9 to 15 inches) long and weigh between 0.7 and 2.2 kg (1.5 to 4.9 pounds). Similar to other crustaceans, lobsters possess a tough exoskeleton that they must shed to grow, a process known as ecdysis or moulting. Young lobsters may undergo this process several times a year, but it reduces to once every 1 to 2 years as they grow larger.

The initial set of pereiopods features a large, asymmetrical pair of claws. The bigger claw, known as the "crusher," is equipped with rounded nodules for crushing prey. In contrast, the "cutter" claw has sharp inner edges and is utilized for gripping or tearing prey. Typically, the left claw functions as the crusher, while the right serves as the cutter.

The exoskeleton is typically blue on top, with spots that merge, and yellow underneath. The red color linked with lobsters emerges only after they are cooked. This happens because, when alive, the red pigment astaxanthin is attached to a protein complex, which is disrupted by the cooking heat, freeing the red pigment.

The European lobster, Homarus gammarus, is most closely related to the American lobster, Homarus americanus. These species share many similarities and can be artificially crossbred; however, hybrids are rare in nature due to non-overlapping habitats. Several features allow for distinguishing between the two species:

Female H. gammarus become sexually mature when their carapace reaches 80 to 85 millimeters (3.1 to 3.3 inches) in length, while males reach maturity at a slightly smaller size. Mating usually takes place in the summer between a recently molted female with a soft shell and a hard-shelled male. The female carries the eggs attached to her pleopods for up to 12 months, depending on the temperature. Females with eggs are referred to as "berried" and can be observed at any time of the year.

The eggs hatch during the night, and the larvae ascend to the water's surface, where they drift with ocean currents and feed on zooplankton. This phase includes three molts and lasts between 15 and 35 days. After the third molt, the juvenile resembles the adult form more closely and begins a benthic lifestyle. Juveniles are seldom observed in the wild and are not well understood, although they are known for their ability to create extensive burrows. It is estimated that only 1 in every 20,000 larvae survives to the benthic stage. Once they achieve a carapace length of 15 mm (0.59 in), the juveniles emerge from their burrows to commence their adult lives.

Homarus gammarus is distributed throughout the northeastern Atlantic Ocean, ranging from northern Norway to the Azores and Morocco, excluding the Baltic Sea. It is also prevalent in most parts of the Mediterranean Sea, except for the area east of Crete, and is found along the northwest coast of the Black Sea. The species' northernmost populations inhabit the Norwegian fjords, within the Arctic Circle.

The species is categorized into four genetically distinct populations: one widespread group and three that have diverged likely due to small effective population sizes and adaptation to local environments. The first is the population of lobsters from northern Norway, known as the "midnight-sun lobster." The populations from the Mediterranean Sea differ from those in the Atlantic Ocean. The final distinct population is based in the Netherlands, where samples from the area are different from those collected in the North Sea or the English Channel.

Efforts have been undertaken to bring H. gammarus to New Zealand, along with other European species like the edible crab, Cancer pagurus. From 1904 to 1914, hatcheries in Dunedin released one million lobster larvae, but the species failed to establish itself in that area.

Adult H. gammarus inhabit the continental shelf at depths ranging from 0 to 150 meters (0 to 492 feet), though they are typically found no deeper than 50 meters (160 feet). They favor hard surfaces, like rocks or firm mud, and reside in holes or crevices, coming out at night to feed.

Homarus gammarus is vulnerable to a disease caused by a specific bacterium. This disease is commonly observed in American lobsters but has only been detected in captive H. gammarus. In these cases, it is possible that the tanks were previously occupied by H. americanus.

Homarus gammarus is traditionally regarded as a highly valued food item and was referenced in a 17th-century English folk song. It can command very high prices and is available fresh, frozen, canned, or powdered. Both the claws and the abdomen of H. gammarus offer excellent white meat, and most of the cephalothorax is also edible, except for the gastric mill and the "sand vein" (gut). The price of H. gammarus can be up to three times higher than that of H. americanus, with the European species being noted for its superior flavor.

Lobsters are primarily captured using lobster pots, though occasionally lines baited with octopus or cuttlefish can lure them out, enabling them to be netted or caught by hand. In 2008, a total of 4,386 tons of H. gammarus were caught throughout Europe and North Africa, with 3,462 tons (79%) taken from the British Isles, including the Channel Islands. The minimum landing size for H. gammarus requires a carapace length of 87 mm (3.4 inches).

H. gammarus is the designated type species of the genus Homarus Weber, 1795, as established by Direction 51 of the International Commission on Zoological Nomenclature. Before this direction, there was confusion since the species had been identified by various names, such as Astacus marinus Fabricius, 1775, and Homarus vulgaris H. Milne-Edwards, 1837. Additionally, Friedrich Weber's description of the genus was initially overlooked until Mary Rathbun rediscovered it, which invalidated previous type species assignments for Homarus H. Milne-Edwards, 1837, in favor of Homarus Weber, 1795.

The type specimen of Homarus gammarus was designated as a lectotype by Holthuis in 1974. It originated from the coordinates 57° 53′ N, 11° 32′ E, near Marstrand, Sweden, which is located 48 kilometers (or 30 miles) northwest of Gothenburg. Unfortunately, both the specimen and the associated data have been lost.

Air Vice Marshal Frank Headlam, CB, CBE (15 July 1914 – 23 December 1976), was a high-ranking officer in the Royal Australian Air Force (RAAF). Born and educated in Tasmania, he entered the RAAF as an air cadet in January 1934. Prior to World War II, he specialized in flying instruction and navigation. In April 1941, he was appointed commanding officer of No. 2 Squadron, which flew Lockheed Hudsons. The squadron was sent to Dutch Timor in December and engaged Japanese forces in the South West Pacific. Upon returning to Australia in February 1942, Headlam held various staff roles and training commands, concluding the war as a group captain.

Headlam held the position of Officer Commanding North-Western Area in 1946 and served as Director of Training from 1947 to 1950. During the Malayan Emergency in 1950–51, he was stationed in Singapore as the commander of No. 90 (Composite) Wing and later at RAF Tengah. He acted as Air Member for Personnel twice, in 1957 and 1959–60, and was awarded the title of Commander of the Order of the British Empire in 1958. Upon promotion to air vice marshal, he served as Air Officer Commanding (AOC) Operational Command from 1961 to 1962, AOC No. 224 Group RAF during the Indonesia-Malaysia Konfrontasi from 1962 to 1965, Deputy Chief of the Air Staff in 1965–66, and AOC Support Command in 1966–67. He was honored as a Companion of the Order of the Bath in 1965. After his assignment in London as Head of the Australian Joint Services Staff from 1968 to 1971, he retired from the Air Force and passed away in Melbourne five years later.

Born to farmers Malcolm and Hilda Headlam, Frank Headlam entered the world on 15 July 1914 in Launceston, Tasmania. He attended <unk> College in Hobart and completed his matriculation in 1932. Despite his parents' objections, he enlisted in the Royal Australian Air Force (RAAF) as an air cadet on 16 January 1934. He received his flight training at No. 1 Flying Training School (FTS) located at RAAF Point Cook, Victoria, and earned his commission as a pilot officer on 1 January 1935.

After completing a conversion course, Headlam was assigned to the Seaplane Squadron at Point Cook. According to the official history of the pre-war RAAF, this squadron was no larger than a flight and was part of No. 1 FTS. It operated Supermarine Southampton flying boats and de Havilland Gipsy Moth floatplanes, among other aircraft. During this assignment, Headlam was promoted to flying officer on 1 July 1935. He also wrote a paper on national defense, suggesting that with strong air and naval forces, including submarines, and fixed defenses, Australia could become nearly invulnerable. Air Force historian Alan Stephens noted that this paper essentially defined the 'anti-lodgment' concept, a recurring theme in RAAF strategic thinking.

In July 1936, Headlam completed a flying instructors course and joined the staff at No. 1 FTS. He was promoted to flight lieutenant on March 1, 1937. Starting in July 1938, he was among six students participating in the RAAF's inaugural Long Specialist Navigation Course, which was conducted by Flight Lieutenants Bill Garing and Alister Murdoch at Point Cook. The course featured several notable training flights that garnered significant media coverage, including a twelve-day, 10,800-kilometer (6,700-mile) round-Australia trip by three Avro Ansons in November, with Headlam piloting one. The next month, he led the three Ansons on a six-day expedition over Central Australia. Headlam completed the navigation course with special distinction. On January 27, 1939, he was assigned to RAAF Station Laverton, Victoria, as a flight commander. He initially served with No. 2 Squadron before moving to No. 1 Squadron on August 29, both units operating Ansons.

After World War II began, No. 1 Squadron took on roles in convoy escort and maritime reconnaissance off the southeastern coast of Australia. Headlam remained with the squadron as a flight commander until January 15, 1940, when he was reassigned to Headquarters Laverton as the station navigation officer. On March 27, he joined the staff at RAAF Headquarters in Melbourne. He was elevated to the rank of squadron leader on June 1, 1940. Just two weeks later, he married Katherine Bridge at St Paul's Anglican Church in Frankston, and the couple went on to have a son and a daughter.

Headlam took command of No. 2 Squadron at Laverton on 15 April 1941 and was promoted to wing commander on 1 July. The squadron, equipped with Lockheed Hudsons, primarily conducted maritime patrols in the southern waters until 5 December, when four aircraft were dispatched to Darwin, Northern Territory, due to concerns over Japanese threats in the Pacific. On 7 December, this group settled at Penfui, near Koepang in Dutch Timor, while the remaining eight Hudsons from No. 2 Squadron stayed on alert in Darwin. The next day, after learning that Australia was at war in the Pacific, a Hudson from Penfui attacked the Japanese ship Nanyo Maru, suspected of being a radio vessel, forcing it ashore. By 12 December, Headlam had moved to Penfui to command both the base and No. 2 Squadron.

In January 1942, No. 2 Squadron's aircraft were stationed at Penfui, <unk> Island, and Darwin. The Penfui unit targeted Japanese ships involved in the Celebes invasion. On January 11, two Hudsons downed or damaged three Japanese floatplanes during an attack on a transport ship, but both were shot down by Mitsubishi Zeros the following day. The Japanese first bombed Penfui on January 26, 1942, and continued to attack regularly, causing damage to some aircraft. The undamaged Hudsons were moved to Darwin, while Headlam and his team stayed at Penfui to support reconnaissance missions from Australia. On February 18, Headlam was instructed to evacuate all personnel except a small group to destroy the airfield with help from Sparrow Force. He returned to Darwin the next day, coinciding with the city's first Japanese raid. Four of No. 2 Squadron's Hudsons were lost in the attack, and the rest were moved to Daly Waters to continue reconnaissance and bombing missions against Japanese targets in Timor.

Headlam stayed in Darwin serving as Controller of Operations at Headquarters North-Western Area Command until 12 May 1942. He was then assigned to Nhill, Victoria, as the commanding officer of No. 2 Air Navigation School, which operated Ansons. In June, No. 97 (Reserve) Squadron was established using the school's personnel. On 20 July 1943, Headlam assumed command of No. 2 Air Observer School at Mount Gambier, South Australia, also operating Ansons. He was promoted to group captain on 1 December 1943 and became the first commanding officer of No. 3 unit, operating Ansons and Fairey Battles from Port Pirie, on 9 December. After passing command of No. 3 unit, he began studies at RAAF Staff School in Mount Martha, Victoria, on 2 October 1944. On 12 January 1945, he was appointed senior administrative staff officer at North-Western Area Command.

In January 1946, Headlam took charge of the North-Western Area. By the year's end, he was posted to Britain, where he attended the Royal Air Force Staff College in Andover and worked with the RAAF Overseas Headquarters in London. Upon returning to Australia in November 1947, he was appointed Director of Training at RAAF Headquarters. In November 1950, Headlam succeeded Group Captain Paddy Heffernan as commander of No. 90 (Composite) Wing. Based at RAF Changi in Singapore, No. 90 Wing managed RAAF units during the Malayan Emergency, including No. 1 (Bomber) Squadron with Avro Lincolns and No. 38 (Transport) Squadron with Douglas C-47 Dakotas. The Lincolns performed area bombing on communist territories and targeted strikes. The Dakotas handled courier flights, VIP transport, and medical evacuations in South East Asia, as well as airlifting troops and supplies in Malaya, and distributing propaganda leaflets. On December 20, Headlam was slightly injured when a No. 38 Squadron Dakota he co-piloted crash-landed at Kampong Aur in Pahang due to engine failure. In August 1951, he was named commander of RAF Tengah, Singapore, while still leading No. 90 Wing. He relinquished command of No. 90 Wing in December 1951.

On February 19, 1952, Headlam took on the role of senior air staff officer (SASO) at the Eastern Area Command in Penrith, New South Wales. During his tenure, the RAAF started updating its fleet with English Electric Canberra jet bombers and CAC Sabre jet fighters. The Air Force also underwent significant organizational changes, shifting from a geographically based command-and-control system to one that focused on function, leading to the creation of Home (operational), Training, and Maintenance Commands. Eastern Area Command, known as an operational headquarters due to its many combat units, was restructured as Home Command in October 1953. In the 1954 New Year Honours, Headlam was made an Officer of the Order of the British Empire (OBE) for his "exceptional ability and devotion to duty." He was promoted to acting air commodore in May. On October 7, 1954, it was announced that he would serve as aide-de-camp to Queen Elizabeth II.

Headlam was elevated to the rank of substantive air commodore on 1 January 1955. In November of that year, he was assigned to the RAAF Overseas Headquarters in London and pursued studies at the Imperial Defence College the following year. Upon returning to Australia, he served as acting Air Member for Personnel at the Department of Air in Canberra from 19 March to 21 October 1957, bridging the terms of Air Vice Marshals Fred Scherger and Allan Walters, and again from 24 August 1959 to 28 March 1960, between Walters and Air Vice Marshal Bill Hely. In this capacity, Headlam was part of the Air Board, the governing body of the service, chaired by the Chief of the Air Staff. He also served as one of two RAAF representatives on a committee led by businessman William John Allison, which assessed conditions of defense service; the committee's recommendations resulted in doubling flight pay, among other benefits. Other roles at the Department of Air included Air Commodore Plans from October 1957 to January 1959, and Director General Plans and Policy from January to August 1959, where he oversaw the RAAF's Directorate of Intelligence. Headlam was honored as a Commander of the Order of the British Empire (CBE) in the 1958 Queen's Birthday Honours, announced on 3 June. In May 1960, he assumed the role of acting Deputy Chief of the Air Staff.

On January 30, 1961, Headlam joined the staff of Operational Command (OPCOM), the successor to Home Command, tasked with overseeing RAAF operational units. In April, he succeeded Air Vice Marshal Val Hancock as Air Officer Commanding (AOC) OPCOM. Headlam was promoted to air vice marshal on May 29. On July 17, 1962, he was stationed at RAAF Base Butterworth, Malaya, and a week later assumed the role of AOC No. 224 Group RAF in Singapore. Air Vice Marshal Alister Murdoch succeeded him as AOC OPCOM. As AOC No. 224 Group, Headlam was in charge of regional air defense and offensive operations during the Brunei Rebellion in December 1962 and the ensuing Konfrontasi between Indonesia and Malaysia that officially began the next month. After divorcing his first wife in 1956, he married Vernon Spence, a widowed social worker, at the Sydney registry office on January 20, 1964. He handed over leadership of No. 224 Group to Air Vice Marshal Christopher Foxley-Norris on November 30.

Upon returning to Australia, Headlam took on the role of Deputy Chief of the Air Staff (DCAS) on 26 January 1965. He was honored as a Companion of the Order of the Bath (CB) on 22 June for his "distinguished service in the Borneo Territories." His term as DCAS overlapped with the Air Force's most extensive rearmament program since World War II and was marked by personnel shortages due to this expansion and Australia’s growing involvement in Southeast Asia's security. Towards the end of his tenure, the first RAAF helicopters were deployed to the Vietnam War, and in March 1966, he traveled to Saigon with Lieutenant General Sir John Wilton, the Chief of the General Staff, to organize the deployment. The previous year, Wilton had advised Air Marshal Murdoch, the Chief of the Air Staff, to send two Iroquois to Vietnam for training purposes; however, Murdoch declined, which left the RAAF helicopter squadron underprepared for its collaborative role with the army upon eventual deployment. Headlam succeeded Air Vice Marshal Douglas Candy as AOC Support Command in Melbourne on 8 August 1966. Support Command had been established in 1959 by merging the RAAF’s former Training and Maintenance Commands. On 1 January 1968, Headlam was assigned to London as Head of the Australian Joint Services Staff and served as an Extra Gentleman Usher to the Queen from 17 November 1970 to 5 June 1971.

After returning to Australia in June 1971, Headlam took some time for resettlement before retiring from the Air Force on August 3. He settled in Melbourne and passed away at the age of 62 on December 23, 1976, following a long fight with cancer. He was survived by his children and second wife. A private funeral was held, and he was cremated at Springvale Crematorium.

M-82 is a state highway in Michigan's Lower Peninsula, connecting Fremont and Howard City. This route runs from Newaygo to Howard City, passing through Fremont and skirting the southern edge of the Manistee National Forest. The current M-82 is the second iteration in Michigan; the first was in the Upper Peninsula around 1919. The Lower Peninsula version has been active since the 1920s. Over the years, the highway has seen various extensions and reductions, with endpoints reaching as far west as New Era or Hesperia. The present route was established in the late 1970s.

M-82 starts at a junction with M-120 and B-96, located west of Fremont at the meeting point of three county lines. M-120 serves as the north-south boundary between Newaygo-Oceana and Newaygo-Muskegon counties, while B-96, running east-west, marks the Oceana-Muskegon county line and heads west from the intersection. M-82 heads east from this junction, traveling along 48th Street through rural farmland and into Fremont. In Fremont, the road becomes Main Street, moving through downtown before M-82 veers south onto Stewart Avenue, leaving the town. The highway curves onto 72nd Street, continuing eastward through more farmland. As it nears Newaygo, the landscape becomes more forested near the Muskegon River. M-82 then takes Fremont Street eastward to meet M-37. The highways join together, crossing the river and entering downtown via State Street. South of downtown, M-82 turns east again, separate from M-37, and follows 82nd Street along the southern edge of the Manistee National Forest. M-82 ends at exit 118 on US 131/M-46, west of Howard City.

The Michigan Department of Transportation (MDOT), as part of its upkeep duties, monitors the traffic levels on its roads. These levels are reported using a metric known as average annual daily traffic (AADT), which calculates the average number of vehicles traveling on a road segment each day throughout the year. In 2009, MDOT's data showed that a section of M-82 west of Fremont had the highest traffic volume for the highway, with 16,532 vehicles per day. Conversely, the lowest traffic count was 4,018 vehicles east of Newaygo. Additionally, no part of the highway has been included in the National Highway System, a network of roads vital for the nation's economy, defense, and transportation.

The existing M-82 has its origins in 1926, originally stretching from US 31 in Hart to the northern intersection of US 131 and M-46 in Howard City. It passed through Ferry, Hesperia, and Fremont, taking over the route of M-41. In late 1936, M-46 was extended to cover the segment between Newaygo and Howard City, creating a shared M-46/M-82 route to bridge a gap in the M-46 path. By 1938, this shared segment became solely M-46, reducing M-82 to the northern junction with M-37 in Newaygo. In late 1947 or early 1948, a new alignment was introduced west of Ferry. Instead of heading northwest to Hart, the route was redirected westward, terminating in Shelby.

Two realignments in 1963 and 1964 altered the western portion of the highway, now running from Hesperia to New Era and bypassing Ferry. A significant change around 1969 redefined the highway designations in Oceana County. M-20 took over from M-82 west of Hesperia, extending to New Era instead of Muskegon. M-120 replaced M-20 south of Hesperia, and M-82 now only spanned from Hesperia to Newaygo. In 1973, the highway length increased when the eastern end was shifted back to Howard City. M-46 was redirected to follow the US 131 freeway from south of Howard City to Cedar Springs and replaced M-57 between Cedar Springs and Casnovia. This change allowed the highway from Newaygo to Howard City to revert to the M-82 designation. The final adjustment occurred in 1978 when the concurrency with M-120 was removed in favor of M-120, and the M-82 designation was shortened to the junction west of Fremont, creating the current highway configuration.

Shikamaru Nara is a fictional character from the Naruto manga and anime series created by Masashi Kishimoto. In the story, Shikamaru is a ninja from the village of Konohagakure and is part of Team 10, which includes himself, Ino Yamanaka, and their team leader, Asuma Sarutobi. Shikamaru is known for being lazy and reluctant to use his exceptional intelligence, a trait Kishimoto appreciates for its laid-back nature. Beyond the manga and anime, Shikamaru has appeared in four of the series' feature films and in various other media, including video games and original video animations.

Various anime and manga publications have discussed Shikamaru's character. Reviewers often highlight his laziness and intelligence, as well as his development into a leader. Anime News Network praised him as "an unlikely hero" within the Naruto storyline. Shikamaru is also very popular among Naruto fans, consistently ranking high in popularity polls. Merchandise featuring Shikamaru, such as action figures, key chains, and patches, has been produced.

Masashi Kishimoto expressed a fondness for Shikamaru, appreciating his laid-back demeanor despite being a genius, and highlighted the contrast with Sasuke Uchiha's smart yet abrasive nature. Kishimoto humorously mentioned that, if he were female, he would marry Shikamaru, believing Shikamaru would likely achieve success in life. When designing Shikamaru's look for Part II, Kishimoto aimed to make him stand out, despite using the same vest worn by other ninjas in the series. To avoid covering Shikamaru's hair, he placed the forehead protector on his arm.

Shikamaru makes his first significant appearance in the series during the Chunin Exams, which are biannual tests for ninjas aspiring to advance in rank. He is a member of Team 10 alongside <unk> <unk> and Ino Yamanaka. Known for his lack of enthusiasm, Shikamaru tries to live life with minimal effort. Despite his lazy demeanor, he is exceptionally intelligent, with his teacher, Asuma Sarutobi, estimating his IQ to be over 200. Shikamaru's skills revolve around the Shadow Imitation Technique (影真似の術, Kage Mane no Jutsu, known as "Shadow Possession Jutsu" in English TV), a signature move of his clan. This technique allows him to connect his shadow with an opponent's, immobilizing them and forcing them to mimic his actions. Throughout the series, Shikamaru learns to manipulate his shadow in innovative ways. By Part II, he can perform multiple shadow-based techniques simultaneously and elevate his shadow to interact with physical objects, such as piercing enemies with shadow tendrils or using them to launch weapons.

Shikamaru enters the exams with a lack of enthusiasm; during his match against the Sunagakure ninja Temari, he manages to defeat her but ultimately concedes the fight due to depleted chakra. Despite this setback, he is the only one among his peers to be elevated to Chunin rank, as the exam overseers were impressed by the strategic insight and intelligence he showed against Temari. As a Chunin, Shikamaru is assigned to lead a team tasked with preventing Sasuke Uchiha's defection to the village of Otogakure. Although Shikamaru's team overcomes the Otogakure ninjas blocking their path, Sasuke still manages to escape.

In Part II of the series, Shikamaru is tasked with tracking down two members of the Akatsuki criminal organization. Despite finding them, the immortal Akatsuki member kills Asuma Sarutobi during the battle, despite Shikamaru's best efforts to prevent it. After Asuma's funeral, Shikamaru, along with the remaining Team 10 members and Kakashi Hatake, seeks revenge for their mentor. While his teammates deal with one of the Akatsuki member's partners, Shikamaru successfully avenges Asuma by defeating the other and ensuring the body is never discovered. After the fight, Shikamaru vows to protect Kurenai and Asuma's newborn daughter. He is later assigned to the Fourth Division with Temari and serves as a proxy general under Gaara. In the series epilogue, fulfilling his personal wish during the final battles, Shikamaru becomes an advisor to the Seventh Hokage Naruto after marrying Temari and having a son, Nara.

Apart from the Naruto anime and manga, Shikamaru appears in seven of the series' films: in the second film, he helps Naruto Uzumaki and Sakura Haruno battle Haido, an idealist seeking world domination with a mysterious power; in the fourth film, he briefly fights a horde of stone soldiers; in the fifth film, he, Kakashi, and Sai search for the Land of Sky's base as they plan to attack Konoha; in the sixth film, Shikamaru, Sakura, and Sai combat the chimera beast summoned by Hiruko; in the eighth film, he joins the fight against the demon Satori; in the ninth film, an alternate universe shows a heavier Shikamaru, contrasting his teammate who becomes the strategist; and in the tenth film, Shikamaru leads a team with Naruto, Sakura, Sai, and Hinata Hyuga to rescue Hinata’s sister Hanabi, kidnapped by an Otsutsuki. Additionally, he appears in the third original video animation, participating in a tournament. Shikamaru is a playable character in almost all Naruto video games, including the Clash of Ninja and Ultimate Ninja series, where he uses unique variations of his Shadow Imitation Technique not shown in the anime or manga. Naruto Shippūden: Gekitō Ninja Taisen! EX 2 is the first game to feature Shikamaru in his Part II appearance.

The light novel "Shikamaru Hiden: A Cloud Drifting in Silent Darkness," authored by Takashi Yano and illustrated by Kishimoto, features Shikamaru as the protagonist and storyteller. Set two years following the Fourth Ninja War, the story follows Shikamaru's role in leading the newly created Shinobi Union as they pursue a rogue ninja who controls the far-off Land of Silence and seeks to establish a new world order governed by ordinary people. The novel also delves into his evolving relationship with Temari, ultimately leading to his struggle to name their child together, several years after the events of the novel conclude.

Shikamaru has consistently performed well in the Weekly Shōnen Jump popularity polls for the series, frequently landing in the top ten and achieving fourth place in one instance. The most recent poll was in 2011, where Shikamaru ranked ninth, positioned between Sasori and Hinata. Merchandise featuring Shikamaru, such as action figures, key chains, and patches, has been produced, showcasing both his Part I and Part II appearances. NTT customers ranked him as their sixteenth favorite black-haired male anime character. Additionally, CyberConnect2 CEO Hiroshi Matsuyama has expressed that Shikamaru is one of his favorite characters from Naruto.

Numerous publications covering manga, anime, video games, and related media have discussed Shikamaru's character. IGN described Shikamaru as a favorite, labeling him "the poster child for any card-carrying member of Generation X" due to his general disinterest and reluctance to fully utilize his potential. In their review of episode 110, IGN commended Shikamaru for overcoming his laziness to assume leadership in the mission to retrieve Sasuke Uchiha, agreeing that his promotion to Chunin was justified. Anime News Network remarked on this development, calling Shikamaru's rise as "an unlikely hero" a highlight of the arc. In a later review of episode 135, where the mission to rescue Sasuke fails and his team is severely injured, IGN praised the "great moment" when Shikamaru cried, relieved that his friends would recover, and vowed to be a better leader. Mania Entertainment's Justin Rich praised his "sheer intellect," deeming him "one of the most fascinating characters in the series" and "one of the few truly brilliant fighters in shōnen anime." Dani Moure, another reviewer from the same site, highlighted his battle with Temari during the Chunin Exams as "one of the better fights involving the supporting players."

Meridian ranks as the sixth largest city in Mississippi, USA. It serves as the county seat for Lauderdale County and is the main city in the Meridian, Mississippi Micropolitan Statistical Area. Located along major highways, Meridian is situated 93 miles (150 km) east of Jackson, Mississippi; 154 miles (248 km) west of Birmingham, Alabama; 202 miles (325 km) northeast of New Orleans, Louisiana; and 231 miles (372 km) southeast of Memphis, Tennessee.

Founded in 1860 at the junction of the Mobile and Ohio Railroad and the Southern Railway of Mississippi, Meridian's economy thrived on the railways and the goods they transported, becoming a crucial trading hub. However, during the American Civil War, General William Tecumseh Sherman devastated much of the city in the Battle of Meridian in February 1864.

Rebuilt following the war, the city experienced a "Golden Age," becoming Mississippi's largest city from 1890 to 1930 and a prominent manufacturing hub in the South, with 44 trains arriving and departing daily. Union Station, constructed in 1906, now serves as a multi-modal center, offering access to the Meridian Transit System, Greyhound Buses, and Trailways, with an average of 242,360 passengers annually. Although the economy slowed with the railroad industry's decline, the city diversified, with healthcare, military, and manufacturing sectors employing the most people by 2010. According to 2008 census estimates, the city's population is 38,232, but the area within a 45-mile (72 km) radius has a population of 232,900, and a 65-mile (105 km) radius includes 526,500 people, with 104,600 and 234,200 individuals, respectively, in the labor force, supporting the city's economy.

The region hosts two military installations: Naval Air Station Meridian and Key Field, which together offer more than 4,000 jobs. NAS Meridian houses the Regional Counter-Drug Training Academy and the state's first Department of Homeland Security. Key Field, named after Fred and Al Key, who set a world endurance flight record in 1935, serves as the base for the 186th Air Refueling Wing of the Air National Guard and supports the 185th Aviation Brigade of the Army National Guard. Additionally, Rush Foundation Hospital stands as the largest civilian employer in the area, with a workforce of 2,610.

The city boasts numerous arts organizations and historic structures, including the Riley Center, the Meridian Museum of Art, Meridian Little Theatre, and the Meridian Symphony Orchestra. Historically, Meridian had two Carnegie libraries: one designated for white patrons and the other for African American patrons. The Carnegie Branch Library, which has since been demolished, was among several Carnegie libraries established for African Americans in the Southern United States during the segregation period.

The city has been chosen as the future site for the Mississippi Arts and Entertainment Center. Meridian is the birthplace of Jimmie Rodgers, known as the "Father of Country Music." Highland Park features a museum showcasing memorabilia from his life and career, along with steam-engine era railroad equipment. The park is also the site of the Highland Park Dentzel Carousel, a National Historic Landmark and the only existing two-row stationary Dentzel menagerie worldwide. Other notable figures from Meridian include Miss America 1986 Susan Akin, civil rights activist James Chaney—who was killed in the 1964 Mississippi civil rights workers murders—and Hartley Peavey, founder of Peavey Electronics based in Meridian. The federal courthouse was the venue for the 1966-1967 trial of suspects in the murder of Chaney and two other activists; it marked the first time a white jury convicted a white official for a civil rights killing.

The land now known as Meridian was once home to the Choctaw Native Americans. However, in 1830, it was acquired by the United States through the Treaty of Dancing Rabbit Creek during the era of Indian Removal. Following the treaty's ratification, European-American settlers started migrating to the region.

Richard McLemore, the first settler of Meridian, received a federal land grant of around 2,000 acres (810 ha) and started offering free plots to attract settlers and boost local development. In 1853, most of McLemore's land was purchased by Lewis A. Ragsdale, a lawyer from Alabama, while John T. Ball, a merchant from Kemper County, acquired the remaining 80 acres (0.32 km²). Ragsdale and Ball, now recognized as the city's founders, began plotting lots for new development on their respective land portions.

There was significant debate over the name of the settlement. Ball, along with the city's more industrial residents, favored the name "Meridian," associating it with "junction." Meanwhile, the city's agrarian residents leaned towards "<unk>," meaning "mad river" in a Native American language, named after a nearby creek. Ragsdale suggested "Ragsdale City." Ball constructed a station house on the Mobile and Ohio Railroad, where the sign alternated daily between "Meridian" and "<unk>." Eventually, the growing presence of railroad workers swayed the decision in favor of "Meridian," which remained on the station sign. The town was officially incorporated as Meridian on February 10, 1860.

Meridian was a modest village when the American Civil War began in 1861. Its location at a critical railroad junction prompted the Confederates to build several military facilities to aid the war effort. In 1864, during the Battle of Meridian, General William Tecumseh Sherman led his troops into the city, obliterating the railroads in all directions, along with an arsenal and vast storehouses. His forces set fire to much of the city's structures. Sherman reportedly remarked afterward, "Meridian, with its depots, storehouses, arsenal, hospitals, offices, hotels, and cantonments no longer exists." Despite the devastation, the city's railroad tracks were quickly restored and operational just 26 working days later. During the Reconstruction era, racial tensions persisted, culminating in the 1871 riot after a fire ravaged numerous businesses.

Following the Civil War, the town flourished and entered its "Golden Age" from 1880 to 1910. The development of railroads in the region bolstered transportation and attracted industries, leading to a population surge. As more people settled, downtown commercial activity thrived. From 1890 to 1930, Meridian became the largest city in Mississippi and a prominent manufacturing hub in the South. During and shortly after this period, many of the city's historic buildings were constructed, such as the Grand Opera House in 1890, the Wechsler School in 1894, two Carnegie libraries in 1913, and Meridian's tallest skyscraper, the <unk> Building, in 1929.

The city experienced growth due to a commission government's initiative to introduce 90 new industrial plants in 1913 and the flourishing automobile industry in the 1920s. Despite the stock market crash of 1929 and the ensuing Great Depression, the city continued to draw new businesses. As escapism gained popularity during the Depression, the S. H. Kress & Co. building, designed to "provide luxury to the common man," opened in downtown Meridian, along with the Temple Theater, which served as a movie house. In 1933, the federal courthouse was constructed as part of a WPA project.

Following a short economic lull at the end of the Depression, the nation entered World War II, which revitalized the significance of railroads. Railways were crucial for transporting gasoline and scrap metal needed for constructing military vehicles, making Meridian the rail hub of the region once more. This period of economic growth lasted until the 1950s, when the rise of automobiles and the Interstate Highway System surpassed the popularity of passenger trains. The downturn in the railroad industry led to substantial job losses, causing a decline in population as workers moved to other regions.

During the 1960s American Civil Rights Movement, Meridian was home to a Council of Federated Organizations (COFO) office and various other activist groups. Local resident James Chaney, along with Michael Schwerner, his wife Rita, and Andrew Goodman—volunteers from the North—worked to establish a community center and conducted classes to empower African Americans in the region to reclaim their voting rights. The activism faced opposition from local whites, leading to racial tensions and violence. In June 1964, Chaney, Schwerner, and Goodman traveled to Neshoba County, Mississippi, to meet with members of a black church that had been bombed and burned. The three disappeared that night while returning to Meridian. After an extensive FBI investigation, their bodies were discovered two months later, buried in an earthen dam.

In the federal courthouse in Meridian, seven Klansmen, including a deputy sheriff, were found guilty of "depriving the victims of their civil rights," while three were acquitted in the Mississippi civil rights workers' murder trial. This marked the first instance of a white jury convicting "a white official in a civil rights killing." The case was reopened by the state in 2005, leading to new charges. Edgar Ray Killen was convicted of manslaughter and received a 60-year prison sentence. Meridian later paid tribute to Chaney by renaming a section of 49th Avenue in his honor and hosting an annual memorial service.

Beginning in the 1960s, with the development of highways that facilitated commuting, people started relocating from downtown to new residential subdivisions in the northern areas. As commercial strip developments began appearing downtown, the city responded by designating various areas as historic districts during the 1970s and 1980s to maintain its architectural heritage. The Meridian Historic Districts and Landmarks Commission was established in 1979, followed by the creation of the Meridian Main Street program in 1985.

Meridian Main Street initiated multiple projects to rejuvenate the downtown area, starting with the construction of a new Amtrak Station in 1997, modeled after the historic train station from Meridian's Golden Age, which had previously been demolished. Additional efforts included the renovation of the Rosenbaum Building in 2001 and the restoration of Weidmann's Restaurant in 2002, alongside promoting integrated urban design. In collaboration with The Riley Foundation, Meridian Main Street also assisted in the 2006 renovation and adaptation of the historic Grand Opera House, transforming it into the "Mississippi State University Riley Center for Education and the Performing Arts."

In late 2007, when ownership of Meridian Main Street shifted to the Alliance for Downtown Meridian, the organization, alongside the Meridian Downtown Association, took the lead in revitalizing the downtown area. The Alliance acts as an umbrella entity, providing support staff and housing to the other two groups, while also serving as a liaison among them. Although there were initial plans to renovate the <unk> Building, these were halted by newly elected Mayor Cheri Barry in early 2010. Currently, the Alliance is dedicated to promoting further development and restoration downtown, aiming to support businesses like specialty shops, restaurants, and bars to enhance downtown activity both day and night. The Meridian Downtown Association focuses on boosting foot traffic by organizing special events, and the Meridian Main Street program aids existing downtown businesses.

Due to Meridian's strategic location as a railroad junction, it has become a hub for hotel development. Even before its "Golden Age," several significant hotels, such as the Great Southern and Grand Avenue, were established before the 20th century. As railroads expanded and the original Union Station was built in 1906, numerous hotels emerged to accommodate passengers and workers. The Elmira Hotel was built in 1905, followed by the Terminal Hotel in 1910. Hotel Meridian was completed in 1907, and the Union Hotel in 1908. The Union Hotel gained recognition on the National Register of Historic Places in 1979, while Hotel Meridian and the Grand Avenue Hotel were acknowledged as contributing properties to the Meridian Urban Center Historic District.

As the city expanded, the hotels mirrored the aspirations of the robust economy, exemplified by the eleven-story Lamar Hotel skyscraper constructed in 1927. The Lamar Hotel, recognized on the National Register of Historic Places in 1979, was repurposed as a county annex building. In 1988, it was designated a Mississippi Landmark.

Constructed in 1931, the E.F. Young Hotel became a key part of the African-American business district that emerged to the west of the city's center. During segregation, it was among the few establishments in the city where African American travelers could secure accommodations.

As the city suburbs expanded during the 1960s and '70s, many hotels relocated away from the downtown area. The renovation of the Riley Center in 2006 sparked increased demand and a movement for a new hotel in the downtown area. Plans were made to redevelop the <unk> Building for this purpose, but restoration efforts were halted due to a change in city leadership. In 2013, the <unk> Preservation Society was established to boost public awareness and support for the building's renovation, organizing first-floor tours and anniversary events.

Meridian boasts nine historic districts that are recognized on the National Register of Historic Places. Among them, the Meridian Downtown Historic District merges two former areas: the Meridian Urban Center Historic District and the Union Station Historic District. These districts showcase a variety of architectural styles predominantly from the late 19th and early 20th centuries, such as Queen Anne, Colonial Revival, Italianate, Art Deco, Late Victorian, and Bungalow.
