Since 1985, Meridian has been governed by a mayor-council or "strong mayor" system. Every four years, the mayor is elected by the entire population. Additionally, the city council consists of five members, each elected every four years from one of the city's five wards, which are single-member districts. The mayor acts as the city's chief executive officer, overseeing and directing the daily operations of the city government. Meanwhile, the city council functions as the legislative body, responsible for establishing policies and approving the city's annual operating budget.

City Hall, situated at 601 23rd Avenue, is recognized on the National Register of Historic Places. Percy Bland serves as the current mayor. The city council features Dr. George M. Thomas from Ward 1, Kenneth Dustin Markham from Ward 2, Barbara Henson from Ward 3, Kim Houston from Ward 4, and Randy Hammon from Ward 5. Pam McInnis holds the position of council clerk. Overall, the city has a workforce of 570 employees.

After Hurricane Katrina in 2005, the city created a Department of Homeland Security (DHS), making it the only local DHS in the state. This department manages an area spanning nine counties. With $2.5 million in grants from the Mississippi Emergency Management Agency and other groups, the department started training law enforcement from other Southern states in passenger rail rescue and offered civilian classes on basic handgun use, Boy Scout first aid, hunting, and firearms training. During crises like Hurricane Ivan in September 2005, the DHS played a crucial role by setting up and supporting shelters for 700 evacuees. Currently, the city leads one of the task forces within the Mississippi DHS, which consists of three nine-county teams.

Led by Police Chief Lee since 2009, the Meridian Police Department includes 115 full-time officers, along with part-time and reserve staff. In 2009, the department's Criminal Investigations Division handled 4,000 cases, half of which were felonies. That year, the number of crimes reported was slightly higher than the 2008 figures. Meridian has been labeled as "the safest city in Mississippi with a population over 30,000." The East Mississippi Correctional Facility, managed by the GEO Group for the Mississippi Department of Corrections, is situated in unincorporated Lauderdale County near Meridian. Anthony Clayton serves as the chief of the Meridian Fire Department, which responded to over 1,600 calls in 2009, including 123 structural fires and 609 emergency service calls.

In Mississippi state politics, the Senate district map splits the city into three parts. The city's northern tip falls within the 31st State Senate District, represented by Terry Clark Burton (R). A section stretching from the southwest to the northeast is part of the 32nd State Senate District, served by Sampson Jackson II (D). Meanwhile, the western and southeastern areas are in the 33rd State Senate District, represented by <unk> Carmichael (R). As for the Mississippi House of Representatives, the city is divided into four districts. The southern and eastern parts belong to House District 81, with Steven A. Horne (R) as the representative. The city's central area forms House District 82, represented by Wilbert L. Jones (D). Encircling District 82 is House District 83, where Greg Snowden (R) serves as the representative. The western part of the city, along with a small northern section, is included in House District 84 and is represented by Tad Campbell (R).

At the national level, Meridian is situated in Mississippi's 3rd congressional district, currently represented by Gregg Harper (R), who has served since 2009. Since 1972, Lauderdale County, where Meridian is located, has consistently voted for the Republican presidential candidate. Before this political shift, white voters in the region typically backed Democratic candidates, as Mississippi was a one-party state dominated by Democrats for many decades after the late nineteenth century.

The city's growth has been shaped by various social and economic influences. From its founding until 1970, the population consistently rose with growth rates ranging from as high as 165% to as low as 0.2%. However, the 1970 census revealed a population decrease, followed by a slight increase by 1980, after which the numbers gradually dwindled until they began to rise again in the 21st century. Between 1980 and 2000, there was a population decline of over 14%. The 2000 census recorded a population of 39,968, with a density of 885.9 people per square mile (342.0/km2). By 2008, the city ranked as the sixth largest in the state, and the population had increased by 2010.

Meridian is the main city in the Meridian region, which, as of 2009, included three counties: Clarke, Kemper, and Lauderdale, with a population totaling 106,139. Within a 45-mile (72 km) radius, the population is 232,900, and within a 65-mile (105 km) radius, it reaches 526,500.

While the city's overall population growth has fluctuated, there has been a consistent increase in both the number and percentage of non-white residents. The only decrease in this demographic occurred between 1960 and 1970, during a significant overall population decline. According to the 2010 Census, the city's racial composition was 61.55% African American, 35.71% White, 0.9% Asian, 0.2% Native American, less than 0.02% Pacific Islander, 0.59% from other races, and 0.89% from two or more races. Hispanic or Latino individuals of any race made up 1.75% of the population.

Based on the 2000 Census, out of 17,890 housing units within the city limits, 15,966 were occupied, with 10,033 being family-occupied. Of these households, 31.1% had children under 18, 36.2% were married couples, 23.3% were led by a female without a husband, and 37.2% were non-family units. Individuals made up 33.2% of all households, and 14.0% had someone living alone aged 65 or older. The average household size was 2.39, while the average family size was 3.06. Since 1970, the average household size has declined from 3.04. The median age in Meridian has risen from 30.4 in 1970 to 34.6 in 2000.

The city's median household income was $25,085, while the median family income was $31,062. Men earned a median income of $29,404 compared to $19,702 for women. The city's per capita income stood at $15,255. Approximately 24.6% of families and 28.6% of the population lived below the poverty line, which included 40.8% of individuals under 18 and 22.0% of those aged 65 and older.

The population of Meridian and its surrounding areas is quite religious, with 65.2% of Lauderdale County residents identifying as part of a religious congregation, compared to the national average of 50.2%. In 2000, among those affiliated, 30,068 (59.0%) belonged to the Southern Baptist Convention, 9,469 (18.6%) were members of the United Methodist Church, and 1,872 (3.7%) were associated with the Catholic Church.

Jewish immigrants from Germany and Eastern Europe played a significant role in the city's commercial growth by establishing businesses and services. Congregation Beth Israel was established in 1868, just prior to the city’s "Golden Age." At one point, Meridian boasted the largest Jewish population in the state, with 575 Jewish residents in 1927. Currently, fewer than 40 Jews reside in Meridian, with the majority being elderly.

Meridian is situated in the North Central Hills region of Mississippi within Lauderdale County. According to the U.S. Census Bureau, the city's total area spans 45.9 square miles (119 km²), with 45.1 square miles (117 km²) being land and 0.8 square miles (2.1 km²) consisting of water. The city is positioned along major highways, lying 93 miles (150 km) east of Jackson, Mississippi; 154 miles (248 km) west of Birmingham, Alabama; 202 miles (325 km) northeast of New Orleans, Louisiana; 231 miles (372 km) southeast of Memphis, Tennessee; and 297 miles (478 km) west of Atlanta, Georgia. The surrounding landscape features cotton and corn fields, oak and pine forests, with a topography of clay hills and the headwaters' bottomlands of the <unk> River.

The city's urban core has altered the natural landscape through grading, yet the outskirts still feature a gentle rolling terrain. Throughout the city, numerous small creeks can be found, along with small lakes and woodlands in the northern and southern sections. <unk> Creek flows through the southern part of the city, branching into Gallagher's Creek, which traverses the city center. Loper's Creek winds through the far western region, while smaller creeks like Shearer's Branch, Magnolia Creek, and Robbins Creek are scattered across the city.

Meridian experiences a humid subtropical climate. During the summer months (June to August), the average high temperature is about 90°F (32°C), while the average low is around 70°F (21°C). In the winter months (December to February), the average high is approximately 60°F (16°C) and the low is around 35°F (2°C). July is the hottest month, with an average high of 92.9°F (33.8°C), and January is the coldest month, with an average low of 34.7°F (1.5°C).

The city receives an average annual rainfall of 58.65 inches (1,490 mm). Rain is distributed fairly evenly over the year, with March being the wettest month, averaging 6.93 inches (176 mm) of rainfall. Thunderstorms, which are prevalent in the summer but occur year-round, contribute significantly to this precipitation. Severe thunderstorms, capable of producing damaging winds, large hail, lightning, and heavy rain, sometimes occur. They are most frequent in the spring, with another peak in the fall, and these storms also carry a risk of tornadoes.

In its early days, the economy heavily relied on the railroads in the region. Around the turn of the 20th century, the city was the largest in Mississippi, boasting five major rail lines and 44 trains arriving and departing daily. The city's economy was not only dependent on the railways themselves but also on the goods they transported, such as timber and cotton. From approximately 1890 to 1930, these rail-based industries made the city a significant economic force in both the state and the region. Although the economy slowed with the decline of the railroad industry in the 1950s, the city adapted by transitioning from a primarily rail-based economy to a more diversified one, now focusing on healthcare, military, and manufacturing as major employers.

Meridian, alongside Lauderdale County and the city of Marion, is supported by the East Mississippi Business Development Corporation. This organization, established in 1996 by local business leaders, aims to boost the region's economic growth. As of April 2010, the city's civilian labor force comprised only 15,420 individuals. However, within a 45-mile (72 km) radius, the population is 232,900, and within a 65-mile (105 km) radius, it is 526,500, with 104,600 and 234,200 people in the labor force, respectively. Consequently, Meridian functions as a central hub for employment, retail, healthcare, and cultural activities. Notably, 80% of Lauderdale County's workers reside within the county, while 90% live within 45 miles.

In April 2010, Lauderdale County had 6,260 individuals working in the healthcare sector. The largest employer is Rush Hospital, with a staff of 2,610, followed by East Mississippi State Hospital employing 1,500, and Anderson Hospital with 1,475 employees. Meridian hosts three hospitals and numerous other healthcare-related facilities. Jeff Anderson Regional Medical Center offers cardiovascular surgery, a Level II neonatal intensive care unit, and a health and fitness center. Rush Foundation Hospital and Rush Health Systems manage the Specialty Hospital of Meridian, providing long-term care for patients needing extended recovery in a hospital setting. Riley Hospital has two centers focused on stroke treatment and rehabilitation. Additional healthcare facilities in Meridian include the Alliance Health Center and East Mississippi State Hospital, which has been operational since 1882.

Retail serves as a significant employer in the county, with 5,280 individuals working in this sector as of April 2010. The city sees nearly $2 billion spent annually on retail purchases. The Bonita Lakes Mall, covering 633,685 square feet (58,871 m²), features over a hundred shopping options, including department stores, specialty shops, restaurants, eateries, and United Artists Theatres. Phase I of the 375,000-square-foot (34,800 m²) Meridian Crossroads shopping center in the Bonita Lakes area was completed in November 2007, significantly enhancing the local retail scene. Additionally, the shopping district on North Hills Street has been expanding, with new retail and office spaces opening near the Highway 19 Walmart Supercenter in March 2007.

The region is supported by two military installations, Naval Air Station Meridian and Key Field, which collectively provide over 4,000 jobs to local residents. NAS Meridian is a training hub for naval carrier pilots and enlisted personnel. It also hosts the Regional Counter-Drug Training Academy, offering narcotics training for law enforcement across several southeastern states. The city, which established the state's first local Department of Homeland Security, leads a nine-county regional response team and a twenty-nine-county regional task force. Key Field is notable for the historic endurance flight by Fred and Al Key in 1935. Today, Key Field hosts the 186th Air Refueling Wing of the Air National Guard and supports the 185th Aviation Brigade of the Army National Guard. The site includes a historical aviation exhibit and houses Meridian's Aviation Museum.

In April 2010, the total number of people employed in manufacturing in Lauderdale County was 2,850. Peavey Electronics Corporation, known for producing guitars, amplifiers, and sound equipment since 1965, has its headquarters in the city. Other local businesses include Avery Dennison, Structural Steel Services, Sara Lee, Tower Automotive, and <unk> Corporation. Additionally, the city hosts four industrial parks.

In the heart of the city, the MSU Riley Center generates income through tourism, arts, and entertainment sales. Each year, the Riley Center draws over 60,000 visitors to downtown Meridian for various conferences, meetings, and performances. Meanwhile, Loeb's Department Store, located on Front Street, has become a historic Mississippi clothing destination, staying within the same family for four generations. Since its founding in 1887 by Alex Loeb, the store has been offering quality men's and women's apparel.

For over a century, Meridian has been a hub for arts and culture, hosting numerous organizations and events. The city's first art organization, the Meridian Art League, was founded in February 1933. Initially, art exhibitions took place at the Lamar Hotel in downtown Meridian. In 1949, the organization became the Meridian Art Association and began showcasing art in various venues across the city. When the Carnegie library at 25th Ave and 7th St closed, the Art Association transformed the building into the Meridian Museum of Art, providing a permanent space for exhibitions. Opening its doors in 1970, the museum now hosts over thirty exhibitions a year, featuring a diverse array of art, from traditional decorative arts to ethnographic and tribal pieces, photography, crafts, and more. Its collection includes 18th and 19th-century portraits, 20th-century photography, and several sculptures, alongside numerous educational programs for both students and adults.

The Meridian Council for the Arts (MCA) was established in 1978 as the official arts agency for Meridian and Lauderdale County. Each year, MCA manages its Community Art Grants program, the annual <unk> Festival, various workshops, and other special events. MCA collaborates with numerous local arts organizations, such as the Meridian Museum of Art, the Meridian Little Theatre, and the Meridian Symphony Orchestra. The Meridian Little Theatre, a prominent subscription-based community theatre in the South, was constructed in 1932 and entertains over 22,000 guests per season, making it the most attended community theatre in Mississippi. Founded in 1961, the Meridian Symphony Orchestra held its inaugural concert in 1962 and completed its first full season by 1963. In 1965, the orchestra featured its first international soloist, Elena <unk>, in performance. The Orchestra has supported the Meridian Public School District in creating its own orchestra and strings programs and has also contributed to the development of the Meridian Symphony Chorus. Dr. Claire Fox Hillard has conducted the orchestra since 1991. The orchestra planned to celebrate its 50th anniversary in February 2011 with a performance by Itzhak Perlman.

The city's former Grand Opera House, constructed in 1889 by half-brothers Israel Marks and Levi Rothenberg, showcased numerous renowned artists and performances, starting with a German company's version of Johann Strauss II's "The Gypsy Baron." Closed in the late 1920s due to the Great Depression, it remained deserted for nearly 70 years. In 2000, a $10 million grant from the Riley Foundation, a local entity established in 1998, initiated the building's restoration, supplemented by $15 million from city, county, and federal funds. Renovation of the opera house was completed in September 2006, reopening as the "Mississippi State University Riley Center for Education and Performing Arts." The Riley Center features a 950-seat auditorium for live events, a 200-seat studio theater, and 30,000 sq ft (2,787 m2) of meeting space, drawing over 60,000 visitors to downtown Meridian each year for its conferences, meetings, and performances.

Meridian is recognized as an architectural gem, being one of the nation's most well-preserved cities from the early 1900s. Architecture students from across the U.S. and Canada often visit Meridian as part of their studies, attracted by the city's numerous buildings designed by renowned architects. Highland Park is home to the only U.S. Southern residence designed by Canadian-born architect Louis S. Curtiss, who is famous for developing the glass curtain wall skyscraper. The Frank Fort-designed building is celebrated as one of the premier Art Deco skyscrapers in the country, often compared to Detroit's iconic Fisher Building. Noted California architect Wallace Neff designed several homes in Meridian and the Alabama Black Belt, which is nearby. With family ties to Meridian and Selma in the thriving railroad industry, Neff accepted commissions in the area during slower periods in California. His designs are primarily found in the lower blocks of Poplar Springs Drive, with one house there often likened to Falcon Lair, Rudolph Valentino's Beverly Hills home. Unfortunately, one of Neff's works was lost to an expansion of Anderson Hospital in 1990, and another burned down in Marion Park in the 1950s. The Meridian Post Office, featuring a fully bronze and Verde marble interior, stands as an exemplary post office from the prosperous 1920s. Originally, it included unique lighting fixtures, which were removed during a 1960s renovation and are now found in private homes on Poplar Springs Drive and in North Hills.

Meridian has been chosen as the upcoming site for the Mississippi Arts and Entertainment Center. The Mississippi Legislature approved the concept in 2001 and pledged $4 million in funding in 2006, contingent upon private donors raising an additional $8 million. In September 2007, the city contributed $50,000 to support the project. The proposed center will be situated on 175 acres at Bonita Lakes and feature an outdoor amphitheater, an indoor concert hall, and a Hall of Fame dedicated to Mississippi artists. This Hall of Fame will be located downtown in the former Montana's building, which, along with the neighboring Meridian Hotel, was purchased for $300,000 in July 2010. To promote the future Hall of Fame, the center introduced its Walk of Fame outside the Riley Center in February 2009, with Jimmie Rodgers, a native of Meridian, being the first honoree. The second star, unveiled in September the same year, honored B.B. King, a renowned Mississippi blues musician. On June 1, 2010, authors Tennessee Williams, Eudora Welty, and William Faulkner were added, followed by Sela Ward on June 24, 2010. The center intends to include many more Mississippi-born celebrities on the Walk of Fame, with potential names such as Morgan Freeman, Jimmy Buffett, Elvis Presley, Conway Twitty, and others.

Another prominent venue in the city for large-scale productions is the <unk> Shrine Temple Theater. This theater boasts a 778-pipe Robert Morgan organ, one of only two Theater Organs still in their original settings within the state. Originally accommodating 1,800 people, the Temple thrived during the silent movie era. At that time, it was among the largest stages nationwide, only surpassed by the Roxy Theater in New York City. Currently, with a seating capacity of 1,576, the Temple hosts various events year-round, including live stage performances, plays, concerts, <unk> Shrine functions, and public screenings of classic films.

Highland Park features a Jimmie Rodgers museum showcasing "The Singing Brakeman's" original guitar and other memorabilia from his life and career, alongside equipment from the steam-engine era. Beyond the museum, there are outdoor memorials and a vintage steam locomotive on display. Meridian boasts a Mississippi Blues Trail historic marker, recognizing the city as Jimmie Rodgers' birthplace and highlighting his role in shaping Mississippi's blues music. Notably, it was the first location outside the Mississippi Delta to receive this honor. Additionally, a Mississippi Country Music Trail marker was installed at Oak Grove Cemetery on June 1, 2010, in Rodgers' honor. Since 1953, the city has hosted a festival each May to commemorate the anniversary of his passing.

The park features a 19th-century carousel created around 1895 by Gustav Dentzel from Philadelphia, Pennsylvania. Known as the Highland Park Dentzel Carousel, it has been operational since 1909, holds the designation of a National Historic Landmark, and is the only two-row stationary Dentzel menagerie in the world. Its housing is the sole remaining original carousel building constructed from a Dentzel blueprint. "Around Town" is a public arts initiative comprising 62 carousel horses, symbolizing the historic carousel. These pieces have been sponsored by local businesses and residents, with their design and painting undertaken by local artists. The horses are displayed throughout the city and county.

The city features several recreational parks, such as Highland Park, Bonita Lakes, and a large lake area. Highland Park offers amenities like picnic shelters, swimming pools, tennis courts, a baseball field, softball fields, and a playground, all accessible to the public throughout the year. Bonita Lakes is a city-owned, 3,300-acre (13 km²) park that includes three lakes, the Long Creek Reservoir, and the Lakeview Municipal Golf Course. It also boasts nature trails, jogging and walking tracks, biking paths, horseback riding trails, pavilions, picnic areas, boat ramps, paddle boats, concessions, and fishing spots. The vicinity of Bonita Lakes also hosts Bonita Lakes Mall, Bonita Lakes Crossing, and Bonita Lakes Plaza. Since 1992, Meridian has hosted the State Games of Mississippi, an annual multi-sport event inspired by the Olympic Games. This organization is part of the National Congress of State Games, which is connected to the U.S. Olympic Committee. During its inaugural year, 1,200 athletes took part in twelve sports, and since then, over 70,000 athletes have joined the Games. In 2009, more than 4,500 athletes participated across 27 sports. Participants in these games can compete in the Southeast Sports Festival, while medalists have the opportunity to advance to the biennial State Games of America.

Originally, the games took place over a single weekend in June, but as more sports were added, the event extended to two weekends. The opening ceremonies are consistently held on the third Friday of June in downtown Meridian. The games are conducted at various sports parks, such as Northeast Park, Davidson Complex, and several other fields across the city. Northeast Park spans 85 acres (34 hectares) on Highway 39 and features ten tennis courts, four softball fields, three soccer fields, an asphalt track, and a large picnic pavilion. The Davidson Sports Complex offers six tennis courts, four softball fields, and a half-mile track. Meridian Regional Airport, situated at Key Field on Airport Boulevard South, is 3 miles (4.8 km) southwest of the city. With a runway measuring 10,004 feet (3,049 meters), it boasts the longest public runway in Mississippi. Operating since 1930, the airport provides daily flights to Dallas/Fort Worth, TX.

During the Great Depression, the city considered closing the airport due to high maintenance costs. However, in 1935, Fred and Al Key, who managed the airport, devised a plan to keep it operational. From June 4 to July 1, 1935, the brothers flew their plane, the "Ole Miss," continuously over the city. Their 27-day flight, lasting 653 hours and 34 minutes, generated significant publicity and funding, allowing the airport to remain open. As a tribute, Key Field is named after the brothers, whose flight endurance record in conventional aviation still stands.

In Meridian, early public education was guided by the 1870 Mississippi Constitution. Between 1870 and 1885, trustees chosen by the City Council formed the Board of School Directors, which managed the schools. Although several schools existed in the city prior to 1884, they were privately owned and served only about 400 students. The city constructed its first publicly owned school in September 1884. The initial public school for black students operated in spaces rented from St. Paul Methodist Church. In January 1888, the Mississippi Legislature revised the city charter to permit the establishment of a municipal school district, and by March, $30,000 in bonds was sanctioned for building new public schools. Using these funds, the Wechsler School was constructed in 1894, becoming the state's first brick public school building for black students.

Starting from its initial district and subsequent expansions, the Meridian Public School District has grown to its current size, encompassing six elementary schools, three middle schools, and three high schools. The city also hosts several private institutions, such as Lamar School, Calvary Christian School, Community Christian School, and St. Patrick's Catholic School. Meridian High School, the primary high school in the district, spans 37 acres (15 hectares) with six buildings and 111 classrooms. It serves grades 10 through 12 and has an enrollment of about 1,500 students.

Meridian hosts two institutions of higher learning. Meridian Community College, established in 1937, is situated at 910 Highway 19 N and provides free tuition for four semesters to graduates of the Meridian Public and Lauderdale County School Districts, as well as to homeschooled students residing in Lauderdale County. Initially called Meridian Junior College and located at Meridian High School, it relocated to its current site in 1965. Following the passage of desegregation laws, the college merged with T.J. Harris Junior College in 1970, which had formerly served African-American students. The institution's name changed to Meridian Community College in 1987 to better represent the broad range of opportunities it offers to a growing community. Additionally, Mississippi State University maintains a campus in the city. In the Fall 2008 semester, the college was attended by 763 students from 33 counties across the state and several from Alabama.

Meridian is home to the Meridian-Lauderdale County Public Library, situated at 7th Street and 26th Avenue. Originally, the city boasted two Carnegie libraries, both established in 1913—one for African Americans and one for whites. In the 1880s, a group of women initiated the Fortnightly Book and Magazine Club to raise funds for a city library. The books they gathered and circulated within the club eventually formed the core of Meridian's library collection. Garnering broad support, the club persuaded city leader Israel Marks to seek financial aid from philanthropist Andrew Carnegie. The library for African Americans was constructed at 13th Street and 28th Avenue on land donated by St. Paul Methodist Church, while the library for whites was set up in a building initially owned by First Presbyterian Church of Meridian members, who sold it to the city on September 25, 1911. Remarkably, the African American library was the only one of its kind in Mississippi until after World War I and remains the sole Carnegie library ever built for African Americans nationwide. Both libraries served Meridian until 1967, when they merged following the Civil Rights Act of 1964, consolidating their collections at the current site. The former white library was transformed into the Meridian Museum of Art in 1970, while the former African American library was demolished on May 28, 2008.

Papa Stour, one of Scotland's Shetland Islands, has fewer than twenty inhabitants, some of whom moved there following a call for residents in the 1970s. Situated west of mainland Shetland and covering 828 hectares (3.2 square miles), it ranks as the eighth largest island in Shetland. The soft volcanic rocks have been sculpted by the sea into a remarkable array of caves, stacks, arches, blowholes, and cliffs. The island and the nearby waters are home to a rich variety of wildlife. The island's western side is designated as a Site of Special Scientific Interest, while the surrounding seas are protected as a Special Area of Conservation.

The island is home to multiple Neolithic burial chamber sites and the remnants of Duke Hakon's 13th-century house from the Norse period of occupation. In the 19th century, the population rose to 380 or more when a fishing station was established at West Voe. Afterward, the population steadily decreased, hitting a low of 16 in the 1970s, but has since increased.

Holm is a tidal island that was used as a leper colony until the 18th century, though it is believed many of the "lepers" might have actually been suffering from a vitamin deficiency. Maiden Stack's name is tied to a 14th-century tale. It is said that Lord Thorvald built a small house at the top, now in ruins, to shield his daughter from men. However, his efforts were in vain, as she was discovered to be pregnant upon leaving; in another version, she and her fisherman lover successfully ran away together. Most of the remaining area features a shallow, stony soil likely originating from glacial till. The island has very little peat, and the volcanic rocks contribute to the relatively fertile soils. The scarcity of peat resulted in 'turf scalping' for fuel, leaving exposed rock areas in the interior.

On June 21, 2008, Stuart Hill, the sole owner and inhabitant of the 1-hectare (2.5-acre) island formerly known as <unk> Holm, which he renamed "<unk> Island," proclaimed its dependence, establishing the Crown Dependency of <unk>. Hill based his claim on a historical marriage agreement between King Christian of Norway and King James III of Scotland from 1468, asserting that the island should be classified as a British crown dependency, separate from the United Kingdom and the European Union. However, this claim was not acknowledged by the United Kingdom.

The island consists of various volcanic and sedimentary rock formations dating back to the Devonian period. During this era, the Scottish landmass was part of the Old Red Sandstone Continent, positioned approximately 10 to 25 degrees south of the equator. The Old Red Sandstone layers, formed between 408 and 370 million years ago, resulted from the erosion of earlier Silurian rocks that had been uplifted by the creation of Pangaea and subsequently deposited into river deltas. The freshwater Lake Orcadie lay on the fringes of the eroding mountains, extending from Shetland to the southern Moray Firth. Papa Stour's structure is primarily composed of volcanic ashes and lavas from this time, including solidified volcanic ash and rhyolite lava bands, and also features a Devonian fish bed at Lamba Banks. Numerous large boulders left by Pleistocene glaciation are also present.

The sea's erosion of the soft volcanic rocks has resulted in a remarkable array of caves, stacks, arches, blowholes, cliffs, voes, and other formations, considered some of the finest in Britain. Among these is the 'Holl o <unk>', a cave that extends through the north-west tip of the island, nearly half a mile long and wide enough to row through. The 'Christie’s Hole' in the southwest is another impressive cave, partially collapsed in 1981. Otters, grey seals, killer whales, and harbour porpoises are often spotted in and around Papa Stour. The island hosts breeding populations of Atlantic puffins, Arctic and common terns, Arctic skuas, northern fulmars, common guillemots, razorbills, curlews, wheatears, ringed plovers, and great black-backed gulls. Additionally, many migratory species have been observed in the area.

The island boasts a rich variety of wildflowers, such as mountain everlasting, spring squill, and the ever-present heather. The western part of the island is designated as a Site of Special Scientific Interest, while the surrounding seas are recognized as a Special Area of Conservation. Additionally, the traditional Shetland Pony continues to be bred here.

Human habitation on the island began around 3000 BC, with evidence of several Neolithic burial sites called "heel-shaped cairns." Although details about the pre-Celtic and Celtic periods are scarce, it's probable that the Norse encountered a religious settlement when they arrived. This is suggested by the island's name, which comes from <unk> <unk>, meaning "Big island of the Papar" (referring to Celtic monks), distinguishing it from Papa Little, located about 12 kilometers (7.5 miles) to the west.

Papa Stour is featured in a 1299 manuscript written in Old Norse, marking it as the oldest surviving document from Shetland. The manuscript narrates a dramatic event at the residence of Duke Hakon Magnusson, who later became King Hakon V of Norway. Near the beach at <unk> Voe, there is a stone circle, remnants of a 'ting' or local assembly. This site was the setting of a duel, which was won by Lord Thorvald <unk>, accused of corruption in the 1299 document and later titled ‘dominus de <unk>’. (His unfortunate daughter's story is mentioned earlier.) The remains of Duke Hakon's 13th-century house are still visible near <unk> Voe.

In 1469, Shetland came under nominal Scottish control, although the Norse "Lairds of Norway" retained their Papa Stour estates until the 17th century. During the 16th century, merchants from Bremen and Hamburg established a summer trading post to purchase fish from the local fleet. By the 18th century, two Scottish lairds, Thomas Gifford of Busta and Arthur Nicolson of Lerwick, owned the island. They managed a successful deep-sea fishing industry, conducted during the summer months using six-oared boats known as <unk>.

The island church, overlooking Kirk Sand in the bay of Fore Wick, was established in 1806. Roughly 300 meters from the current church, there might have been an older chapel site on the headland between the west end of Kirk Sand and another bay. Locals refer to it as the 'kirk,' and the Ordnance Survey identifies it as "the site of a chapel from around the twelfth century." According to tradition, supernatural forces disrupted the construction, with each day's work being undone overnight. Eventually, these forces supposedly moved the cornerstone to the present church location, where construction was successfully completed. Excavations in 2004 uncovered little more than large rhyolite blocks and a piece of whalebone rib, lending some credibility to the oral tradition.

In the 19th century, a fishing station in West Voe was established, and the island's population exceeded 360 people. However, as steam drifters were introduced, fishing declined, and fuel shortages contributed to a population drop from the 1870s onward. During this period, another notable event occurred in Papa Stour's history. Edwin Lindsay, an officer in the Indian army and the son of the 6th Earl of Balcarres, was deemed insane and disgracefully sent to the island for refusing to participate in a duel. He remained a prisoner for 26 years until Quaker preacher Catherine Watson secured his release in 1835. Lindsay's Well is a spring on the island's south side where he was permitted to bathe.

There are notable examples of horizontal water mills, often referred to as Norse or Clack Mills, around Dutch Loch. These structures were originally two-story buildings with turf roofs, built into hillsides to access the upper floor where the millstone was located. Inside, a stationary lower millstone and a rotating upper millstone, powered by water hitting the paddles below, were present. Some of these mills were still operational on Papa Stour in the early 20th century, and there remains a functioning mill on the Burn of <unk>, at <unk> in Shetland's south Mainland.

Like many small Scottish islands, Papa Stour saw its population peak in the 19th century but has since faced a steep decline, similar to Mingulay. By 1970, the island's school had shut down, and the population dwindled to sixteen mostly older residents. However, an ad in Exchange and Mart turned this around by offering a croft and five sheep for free, attracting many applicants. By 1981, the census showed the population had increased to 33. Yet by 2005, the population dropped to 20 due to significant conflicts among residents, leading to several court cases and the departure of some islanders, resulting in the school closing again. By early 2008, the population further decreased to nine after a family of seven left. The 2011 census noted a typically resident population of 15, while, during the decade between 2011 and 2021, the total Scottish island populations grew by 4% to 103,702.

On the evening of March 28, 1930, the Aberdeen trawler Ben Doran sank on the Ve Skerries, located 3 miles northwest of Papa Stour, while heading to the village of Scalloway to deliver its catch. At the time of grounding, the weather was relatively calm. However, it wasn't until the next day that another trawler spotted and reported the wreck. By then, rescue efforts by the coastguard and local volunteers were hindered by worsening weather conditions, making it impossible to reach the skerries. A request for assistance was sent to the Stromness lifeboat in Orkney, only 120 miles away, but it came too late to be of any help. Tragically, all 9 crew members lost their lives in the wreck. Only three bodies were recovered: James Mitchell, whose body was sent back to Aberdeen, and J. Cormack and J.R., who were laid to rest in Scalloway.

In February 1940, the cargo ship SS Highcliffe ran aground on <unk> Holm due to fog. Fortunately, the weather was mild, and only the ship and its cargo were lost. In 1967, the Aberdeen trawler Juniper also ran aground, this time in Lyra Sound beneath 60-meter (200-foot) cliffs. The 12-man crew was rescued by the <unk> lifeboat, with the coxswain receiving the RNLI silver medal for the rescue.

The latest shipwreck at Papa Stour happened on December 9, 1977, when the Aberdeen trawler Elinor Viking, captained by Alec Flett, sank on the Ve Skerries. The Lifeboat tried to assist but couldn't get close enough due to rough sea conditions. At the request of Alec Webster, the Coastguard Station Officer in Lerwick, a volunteer crew from Sumburgh Airport took off in a British Airways Sikorsky helicopter. They successfully airlifted all the crew members to safety within hours, despite the stormy weather. The helicopter crew received several bravery awards afterward. Although there were no fatalities, this event led to the construction of a lighthouse on the skerries in 1979 and possibly inspired the creation of the current Search and Rescue helicopter unit stationed at Sumburgh Airport.

Crofting is the cornerstone of life on the island. Sheep are central to the agricultural economy, but various livestock such as cattle, pigs, goats, chickens, ducks, and geese are also raised. Vegetables are cultivated, typically in sheltered areas surrounded by circular walls, known as 'scrubs.' Fishing persists but remains on a relatively modest scale. There is a post office located at the pier, but no shop is available. Mains electricity was introduced to the island only at the end of the twentieth century. The Papa Stour Project provides Christian-supported housing for men dealing with drug and alcohol issues. Ferries now cross the Sound of Papa to West Mainland in Shetland, with the journey taking 45 minutes. Although the ferry accommodates cars, there is just one short road on the island. For visiting yachts, the four main voes offer good shelter, but strong tides in both the Sound of Papa and the northwest demand considerable caution.

"Angel of Death" is the first song on Slayer's 1986 thrash metal album, Reign in Blood. Slayer's guitarist, Jeff Hanneman, wrote both the lyrics and music, drawing inspiration from Josef Mengele, the Nazi doctor known for his human experiments at Auschwitz during World War II. The song's content resulted in the band being accused of Nazi sympathizing and racism throughout their career.

Although the song "Angel of Death" sparked controversy and contributed to the delayed release of Reign in Blood, it is included in all of Slayer's live albums and DVDs and has been featured in several films. Critics praised the song, with Steve Huey of AllMusic calling it a "classic."

Slayer guitarist Jeff Hanneman penned "Angel of Death" after reading about Nazi doctor Josef Mengele during the band's tour. He recalled, "I stopped somewhere and picked up two books on Mengele. I thought, 'This has to be some disturbing stuff.' When it was time to work on the record, those thoughts were still with me—that's how the lyrics for 'Angel of Death' were created."

The lyrics describe Mengele's medical experiments on prisoners at the Auschwitz concentration camp during World War II. Mengele's studies focused on groups like dwarfs and twins, involving both physical and psychological tests. "Angel of Death" mentions several of his procedures, including surgeries without anesthesia, blood transfusions between twins, isolation tests, gassing, injections with deadly germs, sex change operations, and the removal of organs and limbs.

The line "together, joining heads. Just a matter of time 'til you rip yourselves apart" from the penultimate verse alludes to claims that Mengele stitched twins together, with one being deformed. This accusation, suggesting that "the hunchback was sewn to the other child, back to back, with their wrists also joined," was initially made by Auschwitz survivor Vera Alexander during the 1961 trial of SS officer Adolf Eichmann, known as the "architect of the Holocaust." It was claimed that Mengele "sewed the veins together," effectively turning them into "Siamese twins." The allegation gained further attention when Vera Alexander appeared in the 1985 documentary "The Search for Mengele," which has been referenced by several authors, including Gerald Posner, a Mengele expert.

The release of Slayer's 1986 album "Reign in Blood" was delayed due to the controversial lyrics of "Angel of Death." Initially signed with Def Jam Records, the album faced distribution issues as Columbia Records, the distributor, objected to the lyrical themes and found the artwork "too graphic." Eventually, Geffen Records distributed "Reign in Blood" on October 7, 1986. Despite this, the album was omitted from Geffen Records' official release schedule due to the ongoing controversy.
